today.e: From Middle English today, to-daie, todæig, from Old English tōdæġ, tō dæġe (“today”, literally “on day, day forward”), equivalent to to + day.
today.g: On the current day or date.

toddler.e: From toddle (“to walk unsteadily”) + -er – literally “one who walks unsteadily”, hence a young child.
toddler.g: A young child (typically between one and three years old) who has started walking but not fully mastered it.

toe.e: From Middle English to, from Old English tā, (Mercian) tāhe, from Proto-West Germanic *taihā, from Proto-Germanic *taihwǭ, from *tīhwaną (“to show, announce”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to show”).
toe.g: Each of the five digits on the end of the human foot.

together.e: From Late Middle English together, from earlier togedere, togadere, from Old English tōgædere (“together”), from Proto-West Germanic *tōgadura, *tegadura, from Proto-Germanic *tō (“to”) + *gadar (“together”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to unite, keep”), equivalent to to-₂ + gather.
together.g: At the same time, in the same place; in close association or proximity.

toil.e: From Middle English toilen, toylen, apparently a conflation of Anglo-Norman toiller (“to agitate, stir up, entangle”) (compare Old Northern French tooillier, tooullier (“to agitate, stir”); of unknown origin), and Middle English tilyen, telien, teolien, tolen, tolien, tulien (“to till, work, labour”).
toil.g: Labour, work, especially of a grueling nature.

token.e: From Middle English token, taken, from Old English tācn (“sign, symbol”), from Proto-West Germanic *taikn, from Proto-Germanic *taikną (“indicator, symbol, sign”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to show, instruct, teach”) with Germanic *k rather than *h by Kluge's law.
token.g: Something serving as an expression of something else.

tolerable.e: From Middle English tolerable, borrowed from Middle French tolerable, from Latin tolerābilis.
tolerable.g: Capable of being borne, tolerated or endured; bearable or endurable.

tolerance.e: From Middle English toleraunce, borrowed from Old French tolerance, from Latin tolerantia (“endurance”), from tolerāns, present participle of, and participial adjective from Latin tolerō (“to endure”).
tolerance.g: The ability to endure pain or hardship; endurance.

tolerate.e: Borrowed from Latin tolerātus, the perfect passive participle of tolerō (“to endure”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
tolerate.g: To allow or permit without explicit approval, usually if it is perceived as negative.

toll.e: From Middle English toll, tol, tolle, from Old English toll m or n and toln f (“toll, duty, custom”), from Proto-West Germanic *toll, *tolnu, from Proto-Germanic *tullaz, *tullō (“that which is counted or told, reckoning”), from Proto-Indo-European *del- (“calculation, fraud”).
toll.g: A fee paid for some liberty or privilege, particularly for the privilege of passing over a bridge or on a highway, or for that of vending go

toll.e: From Middle English tolen, tollen, variation of tullen, tillen (“to draw, allure, entice”), from Old English *tyllan, *tillan (“to pull, draw, attract”) (found in compounds fortyllan (“to seduce, lead astray, draw away from the mark, deceive”) and betyllan, betillan (“to lure, decoy”)), related to Old Frisian tilla (“to lift, raise”).

tomb.e: From Middle English tombe, toumbe, borrowed from Old French tombe, from Latin tumba from Ancient Greek τύμβος (túmbos, “a sepulchral mound, tomb, grave”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *tewh₂- (“to swell”).
tomb.g: A small building, or a room within one, for the remains of the dead, with walls, a roof, and (if it is to be used for more than one corpse)

tomorrow.e: From Middle English tomorwe, tomorwen, from Old English tō morgne (“tomorrow”, adverb), from tō (“at, on”) + morgne (dative of morgen (“morning”)), from Proto-Germanic *murganaz (“morning”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *mergʰ- (“to blink, to twinkle”), equivalent to to- + morrow.
tomorrow.g: On the day after the present day.

tone.e: From Middle English ton, tone, from Latin tonus (“sound, tone”) (possibly through Old French ton), from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos, “strain, tension, pitch”), from τείνω (teínō, “to stretch”).
From Middle English tone, ton, toon, from the incorrect division of thet one (“the/that one”).

tongs.e: From Middle English tonges, equivalent to tong (“tool for manipulating things in a fire”) + -s.
tongs.g: An instrument or tool used for picking things up without touching them with the hands or fingers, consisting of two slats or grips hinged at

tongue.e: From Middle English tongue, a late spelling of tong(e), tung(e), from Old English tunge, from Proto-West Germanic *tungā (“tongue”), from Proto-Germanic *tungǭ (“tongue”), from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s (“tongue”).
tongue.g: The flexible muscular organ in the mouth that is used to move food around, for tasting and that is moved into various positions to modify th

tonight.e: From Middle English tonyght, to niȝt, from Old English tō niht.
tonight.g: During the night following the current day; during the evening of today.

too.e: From Middle English to (“also, in addition to”), from Old English tō (“furthermore, also, besides”), adverbial use of preposition tō (“to, into”). The sense of "in addition, also" deriving from the original meaning of "apart, separately" (compare Old English prefix tō- (“apart”)).

tool.e: From Middle English tool, tol, from Old English tōl (“tool, implement, instrument”, literally “that with which one prepares something”), perhaps borrowed from Old Norse tól, but at any rate ultimately from Proto-Germanic *tōlą (“that which is used in preparation, tool”).
tool.g: Any physical device meant to ease or do a task.

tooth.e: From Middle English toth, tothe, tooth, from Old English tōþ, from Proto-West Germanic *tanþ, from Proto-Germanic *tanþs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dónts (“tooth”).
tooth.g: A hard, calcareous structure present in the mouth of many vertebrate animals, generally used for biting and chewing food.

top.e: From Middle English top, toppe, from Old English topp (“top, highest part; summit; crest; tassel, tuft; (spinning) top, ball; a tuft or ball at the highest point of anything”), from Proto-West Germanic *topp, from Proto-Germanic *tuppaz (“braid, pigtail, end”), of unknown ultimate origin.
top.g: The highest or uppermost part of something.

topaz.e: From Old French topace (compare French topaze), from Ancient Greek τόπαζος (tópazos).
topaz.g: A silicate mineral of aluminium and fluorine, usually tinted by impurities.

topaz.e: Various theories. Hobson-Jobson mentions as possibilities a corruption of Persian (from Turkish) top-chi, "gunner", or a connection with topee, from the hats they wore.
topaz.g: A black Catholic soldier in the British Army.

topic.e: From Latin topica, from Ancient Greek τοπικός (topikós, “pertaining to a place, local, pertaining to a common place, or topic, topical”), from τόπος (tópos, “a place”).

tops.g: At the very most; as a maximum.

torch.e: Etymology 1 sense 2.3 (Verbascum thapsus) is either due to the plant’s spike of yellow flowers, or because its leaves and stalks were used to make torches (noun etymology 1 sense 1). Etymology 1 sense 3.2 (“precious cause, etc., which needs to be protected and transmitted to others”) is derived from Latin lampada trādere.
torch.g: A stick of wood or plant fibres twisted together, with one end soaked in a flammable substance such as resin or tallow and set on fire, whic

torch.e: Borrowed from French torcher (“to daub; to wipe; to build or plaster with clay mixed with chopped straw”), from torche (“bundle of (twisted) straw; torch”) (see further at etymology 1) + -er (suffix forming the infinitives of first-conjugation verbs).
torch.g: To point (“fill up and bring to a smooth finish”) (inside joints of slates laid on laths) using lime hair mortar.

tore.e: From Middle English tor, tore, toor, from Old Norse tor- (“hard, difficult, wrong, bad”, prefix), from Proto-Germanic *tuz- (“hard, difficult, wrong, bad”), from Proto-Indo-European *dus- (“bad, ill, difficult”).
Probably from the root of tear; compare Welsh word for a break or cut.
tore.g: The dead grass that remains on mowing land in winter and spring.

torment.e: From Middle English torment, from Old French torment, from Latin tormentum (“something operated by twisting”), from torquere (“to twist”).
torment.g: A catapult or other kind of war-engine.

tormentor.e: From Anglo-Norman tourmentour, from Old French tormenteor.
tormentor.g: One who torments; a person, animal, or object that causes suffering.

torrent.e: Borrowed from French torrent, from Italian torrente, from Latin torrentem, accusative of torrēns (“burning, seething, roaring”), from Latin torrēre (“to parch, scorch”).
torrent.g: A violent flow, as of water, lava, etc.; a stream suddenly raised and running rapidly, as down a precipice.

torrent.e: From BitTorrent and the file extension it uses for metadata (.torrent); ultimately from etymology 1, carrying the notion of the flow of information.
torrent.g: A set of files obtainable through a peer-to-peer network, especially BitTorrent.

torso.e: From Italian torso, from Late Latin tursus, from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos, “Bacchic staff”).
torso.g: The main part of the (human) body that extends from the neck to the groin, excluding the head and limbs.

tortoise.e: From Middle English tortuse, tortuce, tortuge, from Medieval Latin tortuca, of uncertain origin. May be from Late Latin tartarūcha, from tartarūchus.
tortoise.g: Any of various land-dwelling reptiles, of the family Testudinidae (chiefly Canada, US) or the order Testudines (chiefly UK, Australia, New Z

torture.e: From Middle English torture, from Old French torture, from Late Latin tortūra (“a twisting, writhing, of bodily pain, a griping colic;” in Medieval Latin “pain inflicted by judicial or ecclesiastical authority as a means of persuasion, torture”), from Latin tortus (whence also tort), past participle of torquēre (“to twist”).
torture.g: The infliction of severe pain or anguish, especially as an interrogation technique or punishment; (usually in the plural) a technique, metho

toss.e: From Middle English tossen (“to buffet about, agitate, toss; to sift or winnow”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Old Norse (compare dialectal Norwegian tossa, dialectal Swedish tossa (“to strew, spread”)), or perhaps from an alteration of Middle English tosen (“to tease, pull apart, shred; to wound, injure”).
toss.g: A throw, a lob, of a ball etc., with an initial upward direction, particularly with a lack of care.

total.e: From Middle English total, from Old French total, from Medieval Latin tōtālis, from tōtus (“all, whole, entire”) + -ālis, the former element of unknown origin. Perhaps related to Oscan touto (“community, city-state”), Umbrian 𐌕𐌏𐌕𐌀𐌌 (totam, “tribe”, acc.), Old English þēod (“a nation, people, tribe”), from Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂ (“people”).
total.g: An amount obtained by the addition of smaller amounts.

totter.e: From Middle English totren, toteren, from earlier *tolteren (compare dialectal English tolter (“to struggle, flounder”); Scots tolter (“unstable, wonky”)), from Old English tealtrian (“to totter, vacillate”), from Proto-Germanic *taltrōną, a frequentative form of Proto-Germanic *taltōną (“to sway, dangle, hesitate”).
totter.g: To walk, move or stand unsteadily or falteringly; threatening to fall.

touch.e: From Middle English touchen, tochen, from Old French tochier (“to touch”) (whence Modern French toucher; compare French doublet toquer (“to offend, bother, harass”)), from Vulgar Latin *tuccō (“to knock, strike, offend”), from Frankish *tukkōn (“to knock, strike, touch”), from Proto-Germanic *tukkōną (“to tug, grab, grasp”).

touching.e: From Middle English touchynge, equivalent to touch + -ing.
touching.g: Provoking sadness and pity; that can cause sadness or heartbreak among witnesses to a sad event or situation.

tour.e: From Old French tour, tourn, from the verb torner, tourner.
tour.g: A journey through a particular building, estate, country, etc.

tour.e: From Old French tor, French tour (“tower”).

tow.e: From Middle English towen, from Old English togian (“to tow”), from Proto-West Germanic *togōn, from Proto-Germanic *tugōną (“to draw, pull”), from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to draw, pull; to lead”).
tow.g: To pull something behind one, such as by using a line, chain, or tongue.

tow.e: From Middle English touw, from Old English tow- (“spinning”) (in compounds, e.g. towcræft, towhūs, towlic), from Proto-Germanic *tawwą; compare Old Norse tó (“uncleansed wool”), Dutch touw (“rope”). Perhaps cognate with Old English tawian (“prepare for use”), Gothic 𐍄𐌰𐌿𐌾𐌰𐌽 (taujan, “do, make”).
tow.g: An untwisted bundle of fibres such as cellulose acetate, flax, hemp or jute.

toward.e: From Middle English toward, from Old English tōweard, from Proto-West Germanic *tōward, equivalent to to + -ward.

towel.e: From Middle English towayle, towel, towail, towaille, from Old French toaille (“towel”) (modern French touaille), Medieval Latin toallia, from Frankish *þwahilu (“cloth”), from Proto-Germanic *þwahaną (“to wash”).
towel.g: A cloth used for wiping, especially one used for drying anything wet, such as a person after a bath.

tower.e: From Middle English tour, tur, tor, from Old English tūr, tor, torr ("tower; rock"; > English tor) and Old French tour, toer, tor; both from Latin turris (“a tower”), Ancient Greek τύρρις (túrrhis) (Hesychius), τύρσις (túrsis).
tower.g: A tall, narrow structure (significantly taller than it is wide, either standing alone or forming part of a larger structure.

tower.e: From Middle English touren, torren, torrien, from Old English *torrian, from the noun (see above).
tower.g: To be very tall; to reach a high height.

town.e: From Middle English toun, from Old English tūn, from Proto-West Germanic *tūn, from Proto-Germanic *tūną, borrowed from Proto-Celtic *dūnom (“stronghold, rampart”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *duh₂-nós (“lasting, durable”), from *dewh₂- (“to last”) + *-nós.
town.g: A settlement; an area with residential districts, shops and amenities, and its own local government; especially one larger than a village an

tell.e: From Middle English tellen (“to count, tell”), from Old English tellan (“to count, tell”), from Proto-West Germanic *talljan, from Proto-Germanic *taljaną, *talzijaną (“to count, enumerate”), from Proto-Germanic *talą, *talō (“number, counting”), from Proto-Indo-European *dol- (“calculation, fraud”).
tell.g: Mental senses related to determining, reckoning, or perceiving

tell.e: From Arabic تَلّ (tall, “hill, elevation”) or Hebrew תֵּל (tél, “hill”), from Proto-Semitic *tall- (“hill”).
tell.g: A hill or mound, originally and especially in the Middle East, over or consisting of the ruins of ancient settlements.

take.e: From Middle English taken (“to take, lay hold of, grasp, strike”), from Old English tacan (“to grasp, touch”), probably of North Germanic origin, from Old Norse taka (“to touch, take”). Alternatively, inherited from Proto-West Germanic *takan (“to take; grasp, touch”). Both from Proto-Germanic *tēkaną (“to touch”).
take.g: To get into one's hands, possession, or control, with or without force.

tear.e: From Middle English teren, from Old English teran (“to tear, lacerate”), from Proto-Germanic *teraną (“to tear, tear apart, rip”), from Proto-Indo-European *der- (“to tear, tear apart”). Outside Germanic, cognate to Ancient Greek δέρω (dérō, “to skin”), Albanian ther (“to slay, skin, pierce”).
tear.g: To rend (a solid material) by holding or restraining in two places and pulling apart, whether intentionally or not; to destroy or separate.

tear.e: From Middle English tear, teer, teere, ter, tere, tyar, tyear, tyer, tær (“tear”), from Old English teagor, tēar, tæher, from Proto-West Germanic *tahr, from Proto-Germanic *tahrą (“tear”), from Proto-Indo-European *dáḱru- (“tear”).
tear.g: A drop of clear, salty liquid produced from the eyes by crying or irritation.
